subject: Chemistry
title: The Exxon Valdez Oil Spill
description: One-minute skill: The Exxon Valdez Oil Spill.

hook.text: In 1989, the Exxon Valdez tanker hit a reef in Alaska, spilling 41 million liters of crude oil into pristine waters.

buildup.text: Crude oil is a complex mix of hydrocarbons. In cold water, it spreads, sinks, and coats everything it touches.

discovery.text: The spill killed 250,000 seabirds, 2,800 sea otters, and 300 harbor seals. Oil persists in the sediment to this day.

twist.text: Hot-water cleaning actually made things worse—it killed the microbes that naturally break down oil.

climax.text: The spill led to the Oil Pollution Act of 1990, requiring double-hull tankers and better response plans.

punchline.text: One reef, one hull breach, 2,000 km of coastline contaminated. Cold oil doesn't evaporate.

quiz.question: Why was hot-water cleaning counterproductive after the Exxon Valdez spill?
options: It killed the natural microbes that break down oil in the environment
Hot water caused the oil to sink deeper into sediment
The heated oil released more toxic fumes into the air

details.summary: In 1989 the Exxon Valdez tanker ran aground in Alaska's Prince William Sound, spilling 11 million gallons of crude oil into pristine waters. The spill killed hundreds of thousands of seabirds, otters, and seals and demonstrated the near-impossibility of cleaning oil from cold marine environments.
details.whyItMatters: The Exxon Valdez spill catalyzed the Oil Pollution Act of 1990 and mandatory double-hull tanker requirements. It became a symbol of corporate environmental responsibility failures.
takeaways: 11 million gallons of crude oil spread across 1,300 miles of coastline
Cold water slowed natural degradation, extending environmental damage
The spill led to mandatory double-hull tanker regulations in the US

faq.question: Why was the Exxon Valdez oil spill so difficult to clean up?
faq.answer: Cold Alaskan waters slowed the natural breakdown of oil by microbes. The remote location made equipment delivery slow. Rocky shorelines trapped oil beneath the surface. Decades later, oil residue could still be found under rocks in Prince William Sound.

faq.question: What happened to the captain of the Exxon Valdez?
faq.answer: Captain Joseph Hazelwood was found to have been drinking before the grounding. He was acquitted of felony charges but convicted of negligent discharge of oil, a misdemeanor. He was sentenced to community service cleaning Alaska beaches, a punishment many considered inadequate.
